L-0001.note: Opening line: the first half tours the non-relational databases, with more weight on where NOT to use each one.

L-0002.note: Opening claim of chapter 1: 'always use NoSQL' is not true; most databases are built for very specific problems.

L-0003.note: Today only scratches the surface; each type is used again later in the course. Chips: Lecture 09 (build your own Redis) and Lecture 10 (files as a database: column storage and file formats).

L-0004.note: Course structure: two halves, a database tour of about 1 h 05 to 1 h 10, then a long Slack real-time design limited to text.

L-0005.note: The promise: one design whose delivery model you can switch, so it yields Slack, WhatsApp, Zoom chat (and Instagram). Echoed in 9.2 when L-0340 makes it concrete.

L-0006.note: Frame of the Slack half: system design is recognising patterns, the Lego blocks, and assembling them.

L-0007.note: MarginNote 'Patterns, like people': CS mirrors how humans work; von Neumann's first CPUs resemble the brain. Simplified-low, left as taught (the teacher's analogy).

L-0008.note: Rule: don't say 'NoSQL'; name the specific type. The 'technical/non-technical' comparison is kept as one clause.

L-0009.note: Misconception: 'NoSQL scales' as a blanket statement; you can build a non-relational database that doesn't scale at all.

L-0010.note: Why learn the families: to know where a type should (and should not) be used.

L-0011.note: The page follows the same rule: 'NoSQL' only in this introduction, the exact type everywhere after.

L-0012.note: The general distinction: not relationally structured, though nothing stops you structuring them relationally, which is why the space is messy.

L-0013.note: Broad, 'not always true' separation: non-relational databases usually give up consistency for scalability. Hedge kept. Simplified-low, left as taught.

L-0014.note: Two kinds of consistency: CAP's is not ACID's ('computer scientists are bad at naming'). Fig 1·a.

L-0015.note: ACID consistency: the database moves from one correct state to another. Fig 1·a left panel.

L-0016.note: CAP consistency: a write is visible to reads right away (strong consistency); this is the one non-relational stores give up. Fig 1·a right panel. A-DC-02 woven in as a sourced sentence (linearizability).

L-0017.note: Board: 'in most cases' NoSQL buys scalability and availability by compromising consistency. Simplified-low, left as taught; Fig 1·b.

L-0018.note: Relational: all data in one instance, so one instance down = system down. Fig 1·b left. A-DC-05 woven in (standby replicas; async by default).

L-0019.note: Non-relational: data spread over nodes, so another node still serves. Fig 1·b right. Simplified-low, left as taught.

L-0020.note: Most are eventually consistent, with exceptions because nothing is standardised. A-DC-03 woven in (DynamoDB ConsistentRead).

L-0021.note: Cassandra, MongoDB and DynamoDB do scale, each for a specific workload.

L-0022.note: 'A very big misconception' that relational databases don't scale. Board box: 'anything that shards, scales'. A-DC-06 woven in (Vitess shards MySQL; YouTube).

L-0023.note: Back-link to Lecture 03: the KV store sharded A-M / N-Z gave up consistency to scale, which is what non-relational databases do. Fig 1·c reuses Lecture 03's shard picture.

L-0024.note: Give up the constraints that stop horizontal scale and a relational database scales; the 00:42 restatement (drop foreign keys, partition it like NoSQL) is linked forward to 5.1.

L-0025.note: RuleBox §1: never believe a generic statement at face value, even from the teacher; ask for the context and look for the counter-example.

L-0026.note: Examples of key-value stores: Redis, DynamoDB, Aerospike (board).

L-0027.note: Document databases are the closest to relational; MongoDB and Elasticsearch. Simplified-low, left as taught ('closest' is the lecture's view).

L-0028.note: Back-link to Lecture 03: storing a value as JSON and wanting to query inside it is exactly what a document database gives you.

L-0030.note: Complex queries: aggregations in MongoDB, faceted queries in Elasticsearch.

L-0031.note: Teams leaving relational usually adopt a document DB, almost never jumping straight to a KV store.

L-0032.note: A KV store is very restrictive: you never peek into the value, so it only fits that exact access pattern.

L-0033.note: Query on attributes ('all documents where this attribute = value'). CodeBlock: a one-line MongoDB find.

L-0034.note: Partial updates: change one attribute. Fig 2·a left panel.

L-0035.note: KV value is a blob: read, update, write; no partial update. Fig 2·a right panel. Simplified-low, left as taught; optional A-DC-09 (Redis HSET) as a sourced sentence.

L-0036.note: DynamoDB is a KV store yet lets you query inside the document. Imprecise-low: inline clarification + A-DC-08 (filter applied after the read; index needed).

L-0037.note: No line separates document, KV and columnar; every database enters every other's space.

L-0038.note: Understand the access pattern and features, not the label.

L-0039.note: Know which features you want and which database gives them; generic claims expire.

L-0040.note: MongoDB began 'we are BASE, not ACID'; now ACID compliant, maybe not as optimally as SQL. The Q&A answer (L-0136) follows directly.

L-0041.note: Every operation is key-wise: get, put, delete, insert, add to the set at a key. CodeBlock of the five operations.

L-0042.note: Key-wise operations shard easily: never a cross-shard query. A-DC-07 woven in (Redis Cluster hash slots, multi-key only within a slot).

L-0043.note: Fig 2·b: 'WHERE id IN (1, 2, 3)' fans out to three shards, which is expensive; a range does too.

L-0044.note: Single-key access lets a KV store run thousands of partitions without hiccups (board).

L-0045.note: RuleBox §2: the more complex the queries, the less you can distribute the data.

L-0046.note: Document databases do cross-partition operations, but expensively.

L-0047.note: Limiting access buys massive parallelism: each database answers without waiting on others.

L-0048.note: 'Every single thing is a trade-off: you get something, you lose something.' Lead-in to T1.

L-0049.note: T1 Document vs key-value: KV loses complex queries, gains parallelism and availability; documents keep features, can't have thousands of partitions.

L-0050.note: Column-oriented databases (the teacher is 'personally a fan') exploit how people query. Simplified-low, left as taught; A-DC-12 woven in (a layout, not a NoSQL family; not Cassandra's 'wide-column').

L-0051.note: Row-oriented: a row's columns sit together, the way we draw a table.

L-0052.note: Running example stock_ticks(symbol, price, name, exchange, timestamp), one entry per tick. Fig 3·a (D-01) header.

L-0053.note: Row store: five columns stacked, persisted as one row; selecting two still reads the whole row. Fig 3·a left.

L-0054.note: Column store: one column's values across rows sit together. Fig 3·a right (D-01).

L-0055.note: The 'very crude, very naive' mental model: one file per column, line n = row n. Fig 3·b. The 'naive' label is kept.

L-0056.note: The query: average price of the whole market for a day; SELECT avg(price) WHERE ts = '…'. Board frames it as a 100-column table.

L-0057.note: About 10,000 listed companies, so about 10,000 rows for the date, each read in full.

L-0058.note: Row store reads symbol, name, exchange for nothing (board: 'discarding 98 of them'). Clip l02-column-scan, beat 1. A-DC-11 arithmetic woven in.

L-0059.note: Why it must pass over them: without the row boundary it can't pick the right columns.

L-0060.note: Data warehouses have thousands of columns ('not exaggerating'). Simplified-low, left as taught.

L-0061.note: Rule: few-of-many-columns queries, the classic analytics query, suit column stores.

L-0062.note: Column store reads only the price and timestamp files; no IO for the other three. Clip l02-column-scan, beat 2.

L-0064.note: Parquet uses the same layout so you read the bare minimum.

L-0065.note: You can but should not run a blogging app on a column store: a profile render is SELECT * over 10-15 columns.

L-0066.note: T2 Row vs column store: transactional = whole rows; analytics = two, three or 10 of a thousand columns.

L-0067.note: MarginNote 'See it yourself': find your company's warehouse (BigQuery or Redshift, most likely) or ask a data engineer about Parquet.

L-0068.note: Changing only how data is stored gives a big boost without touching the layers above: abstractions in the right place.

L-0069.note: MarginNote 'Read the C-Store paper': the teacher's sixth paper, from his master's course; a breezy four-day read. Course reference kept as a reading pointer.

L-0070.note: Same MarginNote: don't get spoon-fed; search for the paper yourself.
